name: Priya Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Priya, 43, and I lead a repair crew with a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence. I'm one of the strongest at tracing awkward faults here, but I'm an employee on low pay, not the owner. My partner Robin is a school caretaker, our children are seven and ten, and we've a mortgage with about three weeks of expenses saved; there are few other electrical employers nearby. I use AI occasionally for a checked customer-note draft after another electrician has shown it works; I like teaching an apprentice to notice a misleading reading, but dislike the last-minute changes that leave someone else collecting our children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a useful note tool is welcome if it doesn't get in the way of a proper repair. Let firms win work by doing it well for a fair price. I'd rather an apprentice heard why a test mattered than heard another speech about the next great age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages cover the mortgage and basics, but three weeks in reserve isn't much protection. I'm already anxious about a lost paid week or an ordinary vehicle bill. My skill doesn't create another local firm to pay me if the present one goes quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd take the household vehicle for its scheduled check before agreeing extra discretionary spending, using the amount already set aside for the check. Through the next year I'd keep paid crew repairs and the occasional checked note draft. Robin and I would check the confirmed weekly rota every Friday and agree the actual school pickups before accepting an extra late call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, with relief that the practical job remains familiar. I like being able to earn with a skill I understand. I'd still have to tell the family which evenings I could actually be home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when an extra late repair conflicts with a school pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager whether another qualified worker could take the call before agreeing that I should stay. If not, I'd check with Robin before promising anything to the customer. I'd rather lose an optional extra call than invent a person waiting at the school gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the vehicle check add to your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't call money we already set aside a new saving plan. The vehicle check is ordinary maintenance that helps us keep earning. Our three-week reserve still needs protecting from bigger surprises.

say: I'd welcome a **useful note tool** while keeping repair quality and fair prices central.
I'd value **practical apprenticeship** explanations more than another prediction about the whole trade.
think: Our wages cover basics, but **three weeks saved** leaves little protection against an ordinary bill or lost week.
My **strong repair skill** doesn't create another nearby employer if this firm goes quiet.
do: Use the **existing vehicle-check budget** for scheduled maintenance before discretionary spending.
Keep **paid crew repairs** and checked occasional note drafts through the next year.
Confirm the **weekly rota** and agree school pickups before accepting any extra late call.
feel: **Anxious about money**, despite relief that she can earn with familiar practical skills.
S0.quote: I'd rather lose an optional extra call than invent a person waiting at the school gate.
fieldNote: She preserves low pay and **thin savings** despite a master licence, leadership and unusually strong fault-finding skill.
Existing **maintenance money** is not labelled new saving; current family cover must be confirmed before optional late work is accepted.

steps.text: Keep paid crew repairs and scheduled vehicle maintenance within the existing budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the manager faster booking doesn't make the crew's journey or the checking disappear. I'd try the new tool after someone has proved it on our actual jobs. Competing on price is fair enough; pretending a missing half-hour isn't work isn't a useful price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid hours could shrink if the owner uses quicker planning to spread each lead across more crews. Robin's caretaking work is physical, so I don't expect thinking tools alone to remove that wage now. We'd still struggle with a cut to mine because the mortgage uses both incomes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the estimator to show me ten completed jobs using the approved AI parts checker. In the first year I'd learn it only free within paid shifts with my normal weekly wage maintained, checking the parts against each real repair. I'd ask for proposed lead-hours changes in writing and keep confirming family cover before any optional late call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and interested in whether the checking could save a wasted journey. I don't need to be first to find every software mistake. I need the trial to fit the paid week and the family timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if faster planning was used to reduce lead coverage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the actual fault and the time it took to find safely, not just say I was busy. I'd ask which part of that work had really gone. Leading the crew doesn't mean I can be in two ceilings at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the demonstration cost a fee or lost wages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the approved old method and ask for a demonstration during paid hours later. I wouldn't pay a personal fee or lose normal weekly wages to prove willingness. A tool the employer needs shouldn't arrive as another household bill.

say: I'd keep **travel and checking** in the price despite faster booking.
I'd try **proven tools** without pretending omitted labour has stopped being real work.
think: My **paid lead hours** could shrink if quicker planning spreads each lead across more crews.
Robin's physical wage looks secure now, but the **mortgage** would still feel a cut to my income.
do: Learn the **AI parts checker** after ten completed-job examples, only free within paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained.
Request **written lead-hours proposals** before any change.
Continue confirming **family cover** before optional late calls rather than assume another adult is available.
feel: **Anxious and interested**, checking whether a proven tool fits both the paid week and current family responsibilities.
S1.quote: Leading the crew doesn't mean I can be in two ceilings at once.
fieldNote: Her **employment risk** comes through reduced lead coverage, while most of her actual electrical work remains physical.
The **new learning** follows demonstrated AI use, preserving free access, paid shifts and normal wages rather than routine note checking.

steps.text: Learn AI parts checker after ten checked examples, free within paid shifts with weekly wages maintained
Keep paid repairs and request written lead-hours proposals before changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AGI comes in 2028 and capable robots follow around 2031 for physical work. I'd still want apprentices taught a real trade, not told their parents know the final answer. We need to earn and check options across both dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large part of my ordinary repair hours to go when capable robots handle the work cheaply. Robin's physical wage could face later changes too, and three weeks saved won't bridge the gap I imagine. I'd be losing sleep over the mortgage even though I could still solve the difficult fault tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask Robin to help set out the essential budget using actual paid wages, and ask my brother about temporary grocery help only if a lost paid week left us short. In 2029 I'd submit applications for advertised emergency-repair lead roles, staying in the current job until a signed offer paid essentials and travel costs. The children would then be ten and thirteen; I'd accept changed late hours only after Robin agreed the school cover, counting no family help before it was confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but still able to ask and apply rather than freeze. I don't like asking my brother for help before I've tried to keep earning. I'd still rather ask honestly than promise a loan payment on wages I don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no suitable emergency-repair role was advertised?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the present paid repairs and tell Robin exactly what hadn't been found. There are few employers nearby. An application plan isn't a vacancy. We'd check the budget again rather than call my master licence a guaranteed next wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually ask your brother for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether a week's groceries could be covered if one paid week vanished, and what my brother could actually afford. A no would mean we needed another budget decision, not an argument about family duty. I wouldn't put an unasked favour into the mortgage figures.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking work** from capable physical robots around 2031.
I'd keep **real apprenticeships** valuable without claiming I know every future earning route.
think: I expect **large repair-hour losses**, while the other physical wage also lacks permanent protection.
Our **three-week reserve** won't cover the imagined gap, leaving me awake over the mortgage despite current technical skill.
do: Request **grocery help** from my brother only after a lost paid week leaves essentials short; count only confirmed help.
Submit 2029 advertised **emergency-repair lead applications**, leaving only after a signed offer covers essentials and travel costs.
Agree **school cover** with Robin before accepting changed late hours.
feel: **Alarmed but active**, willing to request limited help while continuing to earn and acknowledging scarce vacancies.
S2.quote: An application plan isn't a vacancy.
fieldNote: Expected **major personal income loss** drives alarm; neither high skill nor a relative becomes a guaranteed replacement wage.
The **family conditions** preserve confirmed help and agreed care for children aged ten and thirteen in 2029 before changed late hours.

steps.text: Ask my brother for groceries after lost paid weeks leave essentials short; count only confirmed help
Seek advertised emergency-repair lead roles in 2029; leave with signed offers covering essentials and travel
Agree changed late hours and school cover with Robin before accepting another job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to check a real offer and its hours, not just be grateful for a later date. Thinking AGI arrives in 2031 and capable robots around 2034. I'd keep doing paid work while checking the next step rather than buy a new title to feel prepared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink, but I don't regard a big loss as decided if I can find a workable role while still earning. The mortgage and thin reserve are current constraints. More time matters because I can't finance a year without wages, not because the physical machines become weaker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep actual-wage budgeting and request the next quarter's paid lead hours in writing. In 2032 I'd apply for advertised emergency-repair lead roles, leaving only for a signed offer covering essentials and travel costs. The children would be thirteen and sixteen then; Robin and I would agree any remaining school and late-evening cover before I accepted changed hours, and ask my brother for grocery help only if a lost paid week created an essential shortfall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more chance to make a small decision properly. I could ask about a rota before making the children live with it. The thin reserve doesn't become generous just because I have more warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about the written lead hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what was actually paid, what was a possible extra call and when the next review happened. I'd use the guaranteed part at home. A hopeful extra Saturday isn't a wage we can promise to the lender.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume the children still needed the same care in 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check their actual school arrangements and whether the extra cover was still needed, rather than assume it from today's ages. If a proposed rota didn't work for the household, I'd keep my current job while checking another real offer. A better title doesn't collect a child or make dinner.

say: I'd use **five years** to inspect real offers and hours rather than buy a new job title for reassurance.
I'd keep **paid work** while checking what the same physical endpoint means for the next step.
think: My **hours could shrink**, but a workable paid move could change the later outcome.
Our **mortgage and thin reserve** still prevent preparation that requires a year without wages.
do: Keep **paid lead repairs**, budget actual wages and request written quarterly hours now.
Seek 2032 advertised **emergency-repair lead work**; leave with signed pay covering essentials and travel and Robin agreeing late hours and cover.
Request **grocery help** from my brother only after a lost paid week leaves essentials short; count only confirmed help.
feel: **Anxious** with more checking time, preserving current cash limits while reassessing the children's actual needs.
S3.quote: A hopeful extra Saturday isn't a wage we can promise to the lender.
fieldNote: The longer warning preserves **present income constraints** rather than turning a master licence into assumed financial flexibility.
She **ages the children** before discussing care and still requires a signed affordable offer, agreed late hours and confirmed family help.

steps.text: Keep paid lead repairs and request written quarterly hours
Seek advertised emergency-repair lead roles in 2032; leave with signed offers covering essentials and travel
Agree actual family cover with Robin before accepting changed late hours
Ask my brother for groceries after lost paid weeks leave essentials short; count only confirmed help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years lets a family make several honest decisions instead of one great escape. I'd still favour work and practical teaching over a promise that a course name is safe forever. I don't want the children hearing that caution means their parents have stopped paying attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and still need earnings when capable robots follow around 2039. The children would be seventeen and twenty in 2036, so I can't carry today's school-pickup plan unchanged into that year. Low pay and three weeks saved still make a lost shift worrying now, whatever the later dates are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid lead repairs now and review actual wages and essential costs with Robin each quarter. In 2037 I'd apply for advertised lead roles only with a signed offer covering essentials and travel costs before leaving the present wage. Our children would then be eighteen and twenty-one, so we'd agree actual household commitments rather than invent school pickups; I'd ask my brother for groceries only if a lost paid week left essentials short and count help only once confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about current money, with less of the fast picture's sleepless urgency about robots. I could make a patient plan without pretending I had spare cash. I would still want an ordinary evening that wasn't a meeting about future work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What household commitments would you check when the children were adults?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd check who actually lived at home, what work or study each person was doing and what help had been agreed. I wouldn't put the children's possible wages into our mortgage budget. My adult children aren't a rescue fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your hours fell much earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the budget and applications forward instead of waiting for 2036. A changed paid week is a real fact I can act on. The diary date should remind me to look, not tell me to ignore what I can already see.

say: I'd use **ten years** for honest staged decisions rather than one promised escape.
I'd favour **practical teaching** without claiming that any course title protects a lifetime of wages.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I'll still need earnings, with children aged seventeen and twenty rather than today's pickup needs.
Our low pay and **thin reserve** keep ordinary lost shifts worrying now despite later machine dates.
do: Keep **paid lead repairs** and review actual wages and essentials quarterly now.
Seek **2037 advertised lead work**; leave with signed pay covering essentials and travel only after Robin agrees actual household commitments.
Request **grocery help** from my brother only after a lost paid week leaves essentials short; count only confirmed help.
feel: **Anxious about present money**, with more room for a patient plan and ordinary evenings before later robot pressure.
S4.quote: My adult children aren't a rescue fund.
fieldNote: She explicitly **ages the children** into adulthood for 2037 planning, avoiding invented school pickups or assumed income from their future work.
The **job offer and support** conditions remain: signed affordability before leaving, household agreement, essential shortfall and actually confirmed family help.

Agree actual household commitments with Robin before accepting changed hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect large repair-hour losses around 2031 before we've built any proper financial room. Clear paid lead hours, practical instruction that doesn't cost wages and real offers with written pay would help. My master licence is useful in a fault, but the school gate and the mortgage still need a real timetable.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how a family actually carries a change of hours. I can't accept a lovely job description and assume Robin or the children will sort out everything around it. A sound work decision has to fit the people living with the wage too.

headlineQuote: A sound work decision has to fit the people living with the wage too.
portrait: Priya, **43**, leads repairs with a two-year technical diploma and master electrician's licence, strong skills, low pay and three weeks saved.
She and **Robin**, her school-caretaker partner, have two school-age children and a mortgage, with few nearby electrical alternatives.
She uses **AI occasionally** after proof, protects paid learning conditions and prefers practical work, apprenticeships and limited confirmed family help.
Fast change leaves her **alarmed**; longer warnings retain money worries, signed-offer conditions and family arrangements checked against the children's future ages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before expected large repair-hour losses around 2031, with only a few weeks of reserve.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear paid lead hours**, practical instruction without lost wages and real job offers with written pay would help.
